# UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning

Wenjie Liao Affiliation: Waseda University
Email: [jie3040@akane.waseda.jp](mailto:)    Liangjie Zhao
Affiliation: Adelaide University
Email: [zhaoliangjie55@gmail.com](mailto:)    Zehong Cao
Affiliation: Adelaide University
Email: [Jimmy.Cao@adelaide.edu.au](mailto:)

###### Abstract

Self-evolving methods reduce the need for human-annotated trajectories
by allowing tool-using agents to generate their own training data. Yet
existing methods typically separate trajectory generation from
evaluation, relying on static verifiers that cannot adapt to emerging
failure modes or self-consistency signals that may reinforce errors
shared across trajectories. Jointly adapting planning, execution, and
evaluation offers a promising alternative, but introduces a fundamental
coordination challenge: each component continuously changes the data or
feedback used to train the others. We address this challenge with
UnifiedPlayers, a cooperative framework comprising a Planning Player
that generates tasks, an Execution Player that produces multi-turn
trajectories with Python tool calls, and an Evaluation Player that
constructs executable verifiers. We design role-specific rewards that
coordinate the three players toward a shared learning objective under
GRPO. Across two model backbones and twelve reasoning benchmarks,
UnifiedPlayers outperforms the strongest prior baseline by at least 3.5%
on mathematical reasoning and 3.9% on general reasoning tasks. Moreover,
the learned verifier achieves 84.2% adversarial detection accuracy,
while its reward signal exhibits 2.03$`\times`$ higher per-question
variance than a self-consistency baseline, providing more discriminative
verifications. These results highlight cooperation among specialized
players as a promising path toward self-enhanced tool-integrated agents.

## 1 Introduction

Large language model agents increasingly plan, act, and use tools across
multi-step interactions with their environments ([Yao et al.,
2023](#bib.bib1); [Schick et al., 2023](#bib.bib2); [Wu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib4); [Qin et al., 2024](#bib.bib3)). Training these agents
requires execution trajectories that capture tool calls, observations,
error recovery, and final decisions ([Yao et al., 2025](#bib.bib6);
[Barres et al., 2026](#bib.bib7); [Jin et al., 2025](#bib.bib5)).
Constructing reliable evaluation data requires expert input and careful
review, as illustrated by Humanity’s Last Exam ([Phan et al.,
2026](#bib.bib11)). Existing corpora such as Self-Instruct and UltraChat
focus on instruction following and dialogue rather than executable tool
interactions ([Wang et al., 2023b](#bib.bib12); [Ding et al.,
2023](#bib.bib13)). Obtaining realistic trajectories at the scale
required for reinforcement learning (RL) therefore remains a bottleneck
for agent training ([Liu et al., 2024](#bib.bib8); [Prabhakar et al.,
2025](#bib.bib9); [Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)).

Self-generated data offers a way to reduce this dependence on manual
trajectories. A broad line of work lets language models synthesize
instructions, solutions, or interaction data for their own
improvement ([Zelikman et al., 2022](#bib.bib39); [Wang et al.,
2023b](#bib.bib12); [Qiao et al., 2024](#bib.bib14); [Zhao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib16)). TaskCraft expands atomic tasks into structurally
complex trajectories ([Shi et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)). AReaL-SEA
generates interactions together with per-instance executable verifiers
and reuses them as RL rewards ([Gao et al., 2026](#bib.bib19)). These
approaches reduce the need for manually authored training trajectories.
More recent work trains task generators to adapt with solvers. For
example, Agent0 ([Xia et al., 2025](#bib.bib20)) trains its Curriculum
and Executor policies with group-relative policy optimization
(GRPO) ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib22)). The Curriculum proposes
tool-integrated tasks, while the Executor solves them through multi-turn
code execution ([Gou et al., 2024](#bib.bib40); [Feng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib23); [Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib24)). Their supervision
remains self-referential, because the Curriculum reward uses Executor
self-consistency and tool-call frequency, while the Executor learns from
majority-vote pseudo-labels over the same samples ([Wang et al.,
2023a](#bib.bib21)).
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Related Work ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
compares recent tool-integrated RL, self-evolving agents, and
verifier-based training. Neither signal verifies execution: agreement on
a wrong answer can therefore produce incorrect labels and misleading
advantage updates ([Huang et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)).

Therefore, existing work primarily adapts task generation and execution,
while evaluation signals remain derived from Executor outputs or LLM
judgments ([Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib41)). Simply making evaluation
trainable does not resolve this limitation: once planning, execution,
and evaluation adapt jointly, each policy changes the learning
environment of the other two. Specifically, Planning shifts the task
distribution, Execution changes the resulting trajectories and failure
modes, and Evaluation alters the rewards that guide both. We refer to
this circular dependency as _cyclic interdependence_. Without explicit
coordination, such interdependence can induce degenerate learning loops:
Planning may favor easy, repetitive, or unverifiable tasks; Execution
may reinforce confidently incorrect trajectories accepted by the
evaluator; and Evaluation may collapse to trivial rules that accept all
trajectories, reject all trajectories, or repeatedly generate similar
verifier patterns. These failures can mutually reinforce one another,
increasing internal rewards without producing genuine improvements in
tool-integrated reasoning.

We address this issue with UnifiedPlayers, an
executable-feedback-mediated cooperative framework in which all players
are unified through role-specific rewards grounded in a shared source of
executable evidence ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib25)). The Planning
Player (_Task-Setter_) generates tool-using tasks, the Execution Player
(_Solver_) produces multi-turn trajectories with Python tool calls, and
the Evaluation Player (_Critic-Coder_) constructs executable verifiers.
Specifically, for each reasoning task, we design a fixed perturbation
engine to generate adversarial trajectory variants, while a sandbox
executes every verifier against both the original and perturbed
trajectories. The resulting verdict matrix provides shared executable
evidence of task verifiability, trajectory correctness, and verifier
discrimination. We summarize this shared evidence differently for each
player to construct its role-specific reward, with an additional
code-diversity term for the Evaluation Player to discourage repetitive
verifier patterns. To stabilize learning under cyclic interdependence,
we optimize one player at a time with GRPO while keeping the other two
fixed, ensuring that the policies generating its training data and
feedback remain unchanged within each update block. Based on our
experiments across two backbones and twelve benchmarks, UnifiedPlayers
exceeds the strongest baseline by at least 3.5% on mathematical
reasoning and 3.9% on general reasoning tasks. Its verifiers achieve
84.2% discrimination accuracy, while the resulting rewards exhibit
2.03$`\times`$ the per-question variance of Agent0’s offline
self-consistency feedback ([Xia et al., 2025](#bib.bib20)). Factorial
comparisons show Qwen3-4B-Base attribute gains of 2.5% and 2.3% on
mathematical and general reasoning to effective planning, respectively,
and 3.3% on both to evaluation outcomes. Moreover, fresh feedback
improves performance by 1.5% and 1.7% over a compute-matched control
using feedback from the previous iteration, demonstrating the benefit of
our designed evaluation.

Our contributions are threefold. (1) We introduce UnifiedPlayers, a
cooperative multi-player RL framework unifying planning, tool-integrated
execution, and evaluation through shared executable feedback. (2) We
derive role-specific rewards from a shared verdict matrix produced by
executing learned verifiers and alternate policy updates while holding
the other players fixed. (3) We train executable evaluation with
adversarial trajectory perturbations and improve reasoning across two
backbones and twelve benchmarks, with accurate verifiers and more
discriminative rewards.

## 2 Preliminaries

Multi-turn tool-integrated reasoning. Given a reasoning task $`q`$, an
agent interacts with an environment over multiple turns to produce a
trajectory $`\tau=(a_{1},o_{1},a_{2},o_{2},\ldots,a_{T})`$ ([Yao et al.,
2023](#bib.bib1); [Schick et al., 2023](#bib.bib2)). Each action
$`a_{t}`$ is either a tool call or a final answer that terminates the
trajectory. Tools may include external APIs ([Qin et al.,
2024](#bib.bib3)) or code interpreters ([Feng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib23)). In our UnifiedPlayers setting, tool calls execute
Python code in a sandbox and return stdout, stderr, and exit status as
observations $`o_{t}`$, which are supported by related applications such
as multi-hop question answering ([Jin et al., 2025](#bib.bib5)) and
function calling ([Patil et al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Lu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib29)).

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Reinforcement learning
with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains the policy using explicit
correctness checks instead of learned reward predictions ([Lambert et
al., 2025](#bib.bib28); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib25)). A verifier
$`v(\tau)\in\{0,1\}`$ evaluates $`\tau`$ and provides a binary terminal
reward. Checks include code unit tests, math answer matching ([Cobbe et
al., 2021](#bib.bib26); [Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib22)), and
environment state comparisons ([Yao et al., 2025](#bib.bib6)), grounding
rewards in observable outcomes. A recent work AReaL-SEA ([Gao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib19)), generates verification functions alongside synthetic
tasks and uses them to compute RL rewards. In our UnifiedPlayers
setting, the Evaluation Player learns to generate verifiers for new
Execution Player trajectories and errors.

## 3 Method

Figure 2: UnifiedPlayers Overview. Planning generates tasks, Execution
produces tool-integrated trajectories, and Evaluation writes executable
verifiers. A fixed perturbation engine and Python sandbox map verifier
outcomes on original and adversarial trajectories to a shared verdict
matrix. The resulting role-specific rewards support alternating GRPO
updates for all players.

### 3.1 Unified Cooperation under Executable Feedback

As shown in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Method ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning"),
UnifiedPlayers coordinates three trainable policies through shared
executable feedback. The Planning Player $`\pi_{T}`$ generates a task
$`q`$. Given $`q`$, the Execution Player $`\pi_{S}`$ samples $`K`$
trajectories with tool calls, and the Evaluation Player $`\pi_{C}`$
generates $`M`$ executable verifiers. A fixed perturbation engine
creates $`P`$ variants per trajectory. The sandbox runs each verifier
that parses and compiles on all original and perturbed trajectories. Let
$`\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{valid}}(q)`$ index these valid verifiers and
$`M_{q}=|\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{valid}}(q)|`$. Their binary outcomes form
the shared verdict matrix
$`\mathbf{Z}(q)=[\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{orig}}\mid\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{adv}}]`$,
where rows index valid verifiers, columns index trajectories, and one
denotes acceptance.

We first collect each task’s evidence in a cooperative interaction
record for policy optimization,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\xi(q)=\bigl(q,\mathcal{T}(q),\mathcal{V}(q),\mathcal{T}^{\mathrm{adv}}(q),\mathbf{Z}(q),\bm{\rho}^{\mathrm{red}}(q)\bigr),
``` |  | (1) |

where $`\mathcal{T}(q)`$, $`\mathcal{V}(q)`$, and
$`\mathcal{T}^{\mathrm{adv}}(q)`$ contain the original trajectories,
valid verifiers, and perturbed trajectories, respectively.
$`\bm{\rho}^{\mathrm{red}}(q)`$ contains redundancy scores computed from
verifier source code.

Each player derives its role-specific reward from a different summary of
the shared verdict matrix: original-trajectory acceptance for Execution,
original acceptance and perturbation rejection for Evaluation, and task
verifiability for Planning. This shared evidence coordinates the
players, which retain separate policies and are optimized in turn with
GRPO.Appendix [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Cross-Player Interaction Records and Executable Feedback ‣ Appendix B Methodology Details ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
provides the complete construction of the verdict matrix and interaction
records.

### 3.2 Cooperative Players with Role-Specific Objectives

#### Planning Player.

We use a fixed question prompt to generate a nontrivial multistep task
$`q`$ and a boxed answer used only for data filtering ([Huang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib15)). Its reward favors tasks near the Execution Player’s
capability boundary, valid discriminative verifiers, and novelty,
weighted by $`w_{\text{unc}}`$, $`w_{\text{ver}}`$, and
$`w_{\text{rep}}`$, respectively:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{T}(q)=w_{\text{unc}}U(q)+w_{\text{ver}}V(q)-w_{\text{rep}}R(q).
``` |  | (2) |

Here, $`U(q)=\min(\hat{p},1-\hat{p})`$ measures uncertainty across $`K`$
sampled Execution trajectories, where $`\hat{p}`$ denotes the fraction
sharing the majority answer, while $`R(q)`$ penalizes repetition of
previously generated questions. We define verifier writability as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
V(q)=m(q)\cdot\frac{1}{M_{q}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{valid}}(q)}\rho_{i}^{\mathrm{adv}},
``` |  | (3) |

where $`\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{valid}}(q)`$ denotes the set of valid
verifiers among $`M`$ generated verifiers,
$`M_{q}=|\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{valid}}(q)|`$, $`m(q)=M_{q}/M`$ is the
valid verifier fraction, and $`\rho_{i}^{\mathrm{adv}}`$ is verifier
$`i`$’s adversarial rejection rate. We set $`V(q)=0`$ if no verifier is
valid or no valid verifier rejects a perturbation.

#### Execution Player.

Upon receiving a multistep task $`q`$ from the Planning Player, the
Execution Player interleaves reasoning with Python tool calls, using
each tool output as the next observation until it produces a boxed
answer or reaches the turn limit. Valid verifiers then evaluate the
complete trajectory, with their mean acceptance defining the reward as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{S}(\tau_{k})=\frac{1}{M_{q}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{valid}}(q)}v_{i}(\tau_{k}).
``` |  | (4) |

This averages the corresponding column of
$`\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{orig}}`$. Executed checks replace majority-vote
pseudo-labels ([Xia et al., 2025](#bib.bib20)), so agreement among
Execution samples does not guarantee a high reward.

#### Evaluation Player.

It generates $`M`$ Python verifier candidates, each mapping a trajectory
to a pass/fail verdict and the earliest failing step. Parsing and syntax
checks determine the valid verifier set
$`\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{valid}}(q)`$ before sandbox execution. For each
valid verifier $`v_{i}`$, the verdict matrix yields the original-pass
rate $`\rho_{i}^{\mathrm{gold}}=K^{-1}\sum_{k}Z^{\mathrm{orig}}{i,k}`$
and adversarial-rejection rate
$`\rho_{i}^{\mathrm{adv}}=(KP)^{-1}\sum{k,j}(1-Z^{\mathrm{adv}}_{i,k,j})`$,
where $`K`$ is the number of original trajectories and $`P`$ is the
number of perturbations per trajectory. We further compute redundancy
$`\rho_{i}^{\mathrm{red}}`$ as the maximum source-code similarity to any
other valid verifier. The Evaluation Player reward is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{C}(v_{i})=\alpha\rho^{\text{gold}}_{i}+\beta\rho^{\text{adv}}_{i}-\gamma\rho^{\text{red}}_{i},
``` |  | (5) |

where $`\alpha`$, $`\beta`$, and $`\gamma`$ weight original acceptance,
adversarial rejection, and verifier redundancy, respectively. The first
two terms reward accepting originals and rejecting perturbations, while
the last discourages repetitive verifier code. An accept-all verifier
receives no adversarial reward, a reject-all verifier no original-pass
reward, and repeated templates incur redundancy penalties.

#### Reward alignment across players.

We model UnifiedPlayers as a stochastic game
$`\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{P},\bm{\pi},\mathcal{X},\mathbf{J})`$ with three
players denoted by $`\mathcal{P}={T,S,C}`$. Their joint policy is
$`\bm{\pi}=(\pi_{T},\pi_{S},\pi_{C})`$ and utility vector is
$`\mathbf{J}=(J_{T},J_{S},J_{C})`$, while the interaction process
$`\mathcal{X}`$ comprises tasks, trajectories, verifiers, perturbations,
and sandbox verdicts. Each player maximizes its own expected reward
while the other two policies remain fixed during its update. Cooperation
therefore does not require a shared scalar reward; instead, the players
are coupled through shared executable evidence.

The role-specific rewards align these interactions by discouraging
degenerate behavior from each player. For Planning, easy tasks reduce
uncertainty $`U(q)`$ and repeated tasks incur the penalty $`R(q)`$,
encouraging challenging and novel tasks. For Execution, trajectories
rejected by valid verifiers receive lower rewards, encouraging solutions
that satisfy executable checks. For Evaluation, accept-all verifiers
receive no adversarial-rejection reward, reject-all verifiers receive no
original-acceptance reward, and repetitive verifiers incur a redundancy
penalty. Consequently, improving one player changes the evidence and
learning signal available to the others, creating a cooperative learning
process despite their distinct rewards.
Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 The Objectives of UnifiedPlayers ‣ Appendix B Methodology Details ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
formalizes the corresponding player objectives.

### 3.3 Alternating Cooperative Optimization

UnifiedPlayers maintains separate parameters and role-specific rewards
for each player, in contrast to multi-agent GRPO ([Chen et al.,
2026](#bib.bib46)), which uses shared parameters and a global reward
augmented with role-specific format rewards. In each outer iteration, we
sequentially update Planning, Execution, and Evaluation while holding
the other two fixed. Updated Planning immediately generates tasks for
Execution, and updated Execution generates trajectories for Evaluation.
Because Evaluation is last, its updated checkpoint first supplies
verifier evidence in the next iteration. Later blocks therefore use the
latest preceding-player checkpoints while co-player policies remain
fixed within each block.
Appendix [B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Update Order within UnifiedPlayers ‣ Appendix B Methodology Details ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
details the complete update and evidence-refresh schedule.

For an active player $`p`$ in block $`b`$, the dataset
$`\mathcal{D}_{p}^{(b)}`$ contains groups of $`G_{p}`$ candidate outputs
sampled under the same context. Specifically, Planning samples candidate
tasks from a fixed questioner prompt, Execution samples trajectories for
a given task $`q`$, and Evaluation samples verifiers conditioned on
$`q`$ and the trajectory schema. Their rewards are computed from the
interaction records in
Eq. [1](#S3.E1 "In 3.1 Unified Cooperation under Executable Feedback ‣ 3 Method ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning"),
with each group containing outputs only from the active player. The
advantage $`\widehat{A}_{p}`$ is obtained by normalizing each
candidate’s reward by the mean and standard deviation of its group
(Appendix [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Complete Policy Optimization Definitions ‣ Appendix B Methodology Details ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")).
For each token, let $`\varrho_{p}`$ be its probability under the current
policy divided by its probability under the behavior policy, conditioned
on the same context and preceding tokens. Let $`\bar{\varrho}_{p}`$
denote this ratio clipped to
$`[1-\epsilon_{\mathrm{clip}},1+\epsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}]`$. The GRPO
objective is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{J}_{p}^{(b)}(\theta_{p})=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\min(\varrho_{p}\widehat{A}_{p},\bar{\varrho}_{p}\widehat{A}_{p})-\beta_{p}D_{p}^{\mathrm{KL}}\right].
``` |  | (6) |

The expectation averages over groups in $`\mathcal{D}_{p}^{(b)}`$,
candidates within each group, and tokens within each candidate. Here,
$`D_{p}^{\mathrm{KL}}`$ measures the divergence between the current
policy and its reference checkpoint saved at the start of each outer
iteration, with $`\beta_{p}`$ controlling the KL penalty. Candidate and
token indices are omitted for brevity. Let $`b_{\ell,p}`$ denote the
update block of player $`p`$ in iteration $`\ell`$. We summarize the
three player-wise objectives as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{UP}}^{(\ell)}=\frac{1}{3}\sum_{p\in{T,S,C}}\mathcal{J}_{p}^{(b_{\ell,p})}(\theta_{p}).
``` |  | (7) |

This mean serves only as an iteration-level summary: each objective is
optimized independently within its corresponding block, without
combining rewards or averaging gradients across players. Since group
normalization makes advantage magnitudes incomparable across players or
systems, we instead assess optimization stability using realized KL,
clipping fraction, gradient statistics, policy entropy, and
checkpoint-level performance changes.

#### Player-wise optimization.

During player $`p`$‘s update block, we treat its sampled outputs,
sandbox outcomes, and resulting rewards as fixed records, denoted by
$`\operatorname{sg}[\mathcal{D}_{p}^{(b)}]`$. The other two player
policies, behavior policies, and reference checkpoints are also held
fixed. Under these conditions,
Eq. [6](#S3.E6 "In 3.3 Alternating Cooperative Optimization ‣ 3 Method ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
reduces to a clipped GRPO surrogate over only the active policy
$`\pi_{p}`$. Since the three players have separate parameters, the
iteration-level objective in
Eq.[7](#S3.E7 "In 3.3 Alternating Cooperative Optimization ‣ 3 Method ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
therefore satisfies:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\nabla_{\theta_{p}}\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{UP}}^{(\ell)}=\frac{1}{3}\nabla_{\theta_{p}}\mathcal{J}_{p}^{(b_{\ell,p})}\left(\theta_{p};\operatorname{sg}\left[\mathcal{D}_{p}^{(b_{\ell,p})}\right]\right).
``` |  | (8) |

Thus, each block updates only the active player’s parameters from its
fixed interaction records, without propagating gradients through the
other players or the data-generation process. This establishes the
block-wise optimization structure, but does not imply monotonic
improvement.

#### Block-wise optimization stability.

The stationarity here is conditional on fixed interaction records and
auxiliary evidence, including the verifier pool and question history
used to construct rewards. Within an update block, these quantities are
held fixed, so the reward targets associated with a given record remain
unchanged during optimization. This stationarity is local to the block:
once executable evidence is refreshed for the next block or iteration,
the resulting records and reward targets may change. We further
characterize how far an active policy can move from its reference within
such a block. Clipping and KL regularization discourage large policy
updates but do not impose a hard constraint. For a fixed context
distribution, let $`\bar{D}_{\mathrm{KL},p}`$ and $`\bar{T}_{p}`$ denote
the average KL divergence and total variation distance, respectively,
between the updated and reference output distributions. If
$`\bar{D}_{\mathrm{KL},p}\leq\delta_{p}`$, Pinsker’s inequality gives
$`\bar{T}_{p}\leq\sqrt{\delta_{p}/2}.`$ This conditional result assumes
output-distribution KL and does not follow from the token-level KL
training diagnostic.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

#### Implementation Details.

We evaluate UnifiedPlayers on two open-source base models,
Qwen3-4B-Base ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib30)) and
MiMo-7B-Base ([Xiaomi LLM-Core Team, 2025](#bib.bib38)), with all three
policies initialized from the same backbone. The framework is
implemented on top of VeRL ([Sheng et al., 2025](#bib.bib31)) with a
sandboxed Python interpreter provided by VeRL-Tool ([Jiang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib42)) that executes the Execution Player’s code blocks in a
subprocess and returns their standard output as the next observation.
For each Planning Player task, we sample $`K=8`$ Execution Player
trajectories and ask the Evaluation Player to write $`M=4`$ Python
verifiers, each restricted to the standard library with a strict
per-call timeout. The perturbation engine applies all five mutation
rules independently, and the sandbox runs every verifier against the
original and the five adversarial variants. The Evaluation Player reward
then combines these verdicts with coefficients $`\alpha=0.4`$,
$`\beta=0.5`$, $`\gamma=0.1`$ for the original-pass,
adversarial-rejection, and redundancy terms. Each outer iteration
consists of three sequential GRPO update blocks, one per policy, and we
run three outer iterations.

#### Baseline Methods and Evaluation Datasets.

Our six baselines comprise two untrained references, Vanilla and
Tool-augmented, three other self-evolving frameworks, Absolute
Zero ([Zhao et al., 2025](#bib.bib16)), R-Zero ([Huang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib15)), and Socratic-Zero ([Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib17)),
and the two-player Agent0 framework ([Xia et al., 2025](#bib.bib20)).
Vanilla evaluates the original backbone without tools, whereas
Tool-augmented enables the same Python tool interface at inference
without RL training. We use our reimplementations for all baselines and
evaluate them with the same backbone-specific prompts, decoding
settings, benchmark splits, and tool sandbox whenever the method uses
tools. We evaluate seven math benchmarks (AMC, MATH ([Hendrycks et al.,
2021](#bib.bib32)), GSM8K ([Cobbe et al., 2021](#bib.bib26)),
Minerva ([Lewkowycz et al., 2022](#bib.bib33)), Olympiad-Bench ([He et
al., 2024](#bib.bib34)), AIME24, AIME25) and five general-domain
benchmarks (SuperGPQA ([M-A-P Team et al., 2025](#bib.bib35)),
MMLU-Pro ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib36)), BBEH ([Kazemi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib37)), GPQA-D ([Rein et al., 2024](#bib.bib44)),
HumanEval ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib45))), using greedy pass@1 except
mean@32 for AMC and AIME.

### 4.2 Main Performance Results

Tables [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Block-wise optimization stability. ‣ 3.3 Alternating Cooperative Optimization ‣ 3 Method ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
and [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Implementation Details. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
report results across seven mathematical and five general-domain
reasoning benchmarks. UnifiedPlayers achieves the best average
performance on both model backbones, with consistent gains across
individual benchmarks. On mathematical reasoning, UnifiedPlayers obtains
average scores of 56.4 with Qwen3-4B-Base and 64.6 with MiMo-7B-Base,
outperforming Agent0, the strongest baseline, by 3.7 and 3.6,
respectively. With Qwen3-4B-Base, it further surpasses the
Tool-augmented reference by 12.4 on average, with substantial gains on
challenging benchmarks such as AIME24 and AIME25.
Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")(b)
further shows an average improvement of 10.9 over this reference across
five representative math benchmarks. Furthermore, across the five
general-domain benchmarks, UnifiedPlayers achieves averages of 46.1 and
41.2 on Qwen3-4B-Base and MiMo-7B-Base, respectively, improving over
Agent0 by 4.0 and 3.9. A particularly notable gain appears on BBEH with
Qwen3-4B-Base, where all prior baselines score below 12. Importantly,
although the Planning Player generates only mathematical tasks during
training, the consistent improvements across general-domain benchmarks
indicate transfer beyond the training distribution.

### 4.3 Ablation Studies

#### Individual Player contributions.

Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Implementation Details. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
reports a $`2\times 2`$ factorial study on Qwen3-4B-Base, where
Execution is always trained while Planning and Evaluation are
independently trained or frozen under the same generation settings. All
configurations use three outer iterations, matched task and sampling
budgets, and three paired seeds, without reallocating saved compute to
Execution. Averaged over the other player’s setting, training Planning
improves mathematical and general reasoning by 2.5 and 2.3,
respectively, while training Evaluation yields larger gains of 3.3 on
both domains. Their interaction contributes an additional 0.4 on math
and 1.0 on general reasoning, suggesting complementarity without
establishing statistically significant super-additivity.
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Player Coordination Protocol ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Metrics ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
details the paired contrasts and coordination control.

#### Fresh vs. stale feedback.

We examine whether sharing updated checkpoints within each iteration
improves cross-player coordination. UnifiedPlayers immediately uses each
updated player to generate fresh feedback for the next, whereas the
stale-feedback control delays all updated checkpoints until the next
iteration. With matched players, compute, rewards, sampling, and update
budgets, fresh feedback improves mathematical and general reasoning by
1.5 and 1.7, respectively. These results support the benefit of
within-iteration feedback refresh, while isolating feedback freshness
rather than comparing against all independent training strategies.

#### Component ablations.

All players remain trainable while we vary feedback components and the
training schedule
(Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Individual Player contributions. ‣ 4.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")).
One outer iteration causes the largest drop, 9.0 on math and 8.1 on
general reasoning. Removing the Perturbation Engine lowers both averages
by 4.8. Using one verifier or removing $`V(q)`$ from the Planning reward
reduces performance by about two points.
Tables [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Implementation Details. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
and [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Individual Player contributions. ‣ 4.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
distinguish adaptive player contributions from component effects. Both
roles contribute, while adversarial verifier training and repeated outer
iterations have the largest component effects. These comparisons
identify no player as the sole contributor.
Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Additional Results and Analysis ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
provides iteration results and analyses of perturbation subsets,
verifier-pool size, and reward weights.

### 4.4 Optimization Stability

Because group normalization rescales advantages, we compare Execution
Player diagnostics instead
(Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Individual Player contributions. ‣ 4.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")).
Full UnifiedPlayers has lower gradient variability, realized KL,
clipping frequency, and maximum checkpoint decline than all three
controls. Its median pre-clipping gradient norm is 0.73, KL is 0.014,
and clipping fraction is 0.09. Evaluated every 50 updates on a fixed
256-question pool excluded from model selection, its largest checkpoint
decline is 0.6. However, entropy retention is lower at 87%, and negative
steps are slightly more frequent than with Execution + Evaluation. These
findings suggest reduced variability on several metrics, but do not
establish uniformly better stability or convergence. Further details
appear in
Appendix [D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Optimization Stability Diagnostics ‣ Appendix D Experimental Setup Details ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning").

### 4.5 Mechanism Analysis and Qualitative Case Study

Across three Qwen3-4B-Base iterations
(Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")(a)),
Execution accuracy rises from 52.5% to 63.3%, Evaluation adversarial
rejection from 31% to 79%, and Planning uncertainty $`U(q)`$ from 0.18
to 0.39, indicating harder tasks.
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Implementation Details. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
isolates player contributions and fresh coordination. On a shared
question pool, UnifiedPlayers yields 2.03$`\times`$ the reward variance
of offline Agent0 self-consistency
(Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Individual Player contributions. ‣ 4.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")(a,b)),
while the Evaluation Player generates over 95% of top-scoring verifiers.
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Individual Player contributions. ‣ 4.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")(c)
shows 84.2% accuracy in distinguishing original from perturbed
trajectories, approaching GPT-4o’s 90.8% without external training APIs.
This indicates differentiated feedback.

## 5 Conclusion

UnifiedPlayers coordinates Planning, Execution, and Evaluation through
shared executable feedback, while maintaining separate rewards,
parameters, and alternating GRPO updates. Across two backbones and
twelve benchmarks, it consistently outperforms the strongest baselines,
while learned verifiers reach 84.2% discrimination accuracy without
external API calls during training. Factorial and fresh-versus-stale
comparisons further support the contributions of adaptive players and
within-iteration feedback. Future work will explore adaptive adversarial
generation, larger models and broader agent settings, and more efficient
sandbox evaluation.

## Appendix A Related Work

### A.1 Tool-Integrated Reasoning

Tool-integrated reasoning enables language models to combine
natural-language reasoning with external computation. Early systems such
as ToRA use tool-augmented trajectories to improve mathematical
reasoning, while ReTool and TIRL apply reinforcement learning to
multi-turn tool use ([Gou et al., 2024](#bib.bib40); [Feng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib23); [Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib24)). Recent methods
extend this direction through different reward and training designs.
ToRL studies scalable reinforcement learning for computational tool use,
and AutoTIR combines outcome and process signals to encourage autonomous
tool invocation ([Li et al., 2025b](#bib.bib48); [Wei et al.,
2025](#bib.bib47)). Tool-Star supports multi-tool reasoning through
hierarchical rewards and self-critic feedback ([Dong et al.,
2025](#bib.bib50)), while Nemotron-Research-Tool-N1 uses format and
functional-correctness rewards to train tool-using reasoning
models ([Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib51)).

Other studies focus on the optimization challenges of multi-turn tool
use. SimpleTIR removes void-turn trajectories that provide ineffective
learning signals during end-to-end reinforcement learning ([Xue et al.,
2026](#bib.bib49)). Understanding Tool-Integrated Reasoning analyzes the
capabilities required for effective tool use and proposes adaptive
optimization mechanisms for more stable training ([Lin and Xu,
2025](#bib.bib55)). These methods primarily improve the tool-using
execution policy. UnifiedPlayers instead studies the coupled setting in
which task generation, tool-integrated execution, and executable
evaluation are all adaptive.

### A.2 Self-Generated Data and Adaptive Exploration

Self-generated training reduces dependence on manually constructed
demonstrations. Self-Instruct, STaR, and AutoAct generate instructions,
reasoning traces, or agent interactions for subsequent training ([Wang
et al., 2023b](#bib.bib12); [Zelikman et al., 2022](#bib.bib39); [Qiao
et al., 2024](#bib.bib14)). More recent self-evolving methods jointly
adapt parts of the data-generation process. Absolute Zero, R-Zero, and
Socratic-Zero generate reasoning tasks or feedback without external
training data ([Zhao et al., 2025](#bib.bib16); [Huang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib15); [Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib17)). Agent0 jointly
trains a Curriculum policy and an Executor, while TaskCraft generates
structurally complex agent tasks ([Xia et al., 2025](#bib.bib20); [Shi
et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)). AReaL-SEA synthesizes interactions together
with executable verification functions and uses their outcomes as
reinforcement-learning rewards ([Gao et al., 2026](#bib.bib19)).

Related work also improves exploration and experience selection. SPORT
forms a multimodal loop of task synthesis, trajectory exploration,
verifier feedback, and step-wise preference tuning ([Li et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib54)). E3-TIR combines complementary experiences to
increase trajectory diversity and mitigate mode collapse in
tool-integrated reinforcement learning ([Guo et al., 2026](#bib.bib52)).
RAPO retrieves prior interaction trajectories to expand exploration
under sparse rewards ([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib53)). These
approaches improve the tasks or experiences used to train an agent.
UnifiedPlayers focuses on a different question: how three adaptive
policies can coordinate when each changes the evidence or feedback
available to the others.

### A.3 Executable Verification and Multi-Player Optimization

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards replaces learned reward
predictions with explicit correctness checks, including answer matching,
unit tests, and environment-state validation ([Cobbe et al.,
2021](#bib.bib26); [Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib22); [Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib25)). This approach provides reliable supervision when a
suitable verifier is available, but manually defining checks for newly
generated tasks can be costly. AReaL-SEA addresses this issue by
generating task-specific verification functions, while
Nemotron-Research-Tool-N1 incorporates rule-based functional checks into
tool-use training ([Gao et al., 2026](#bib.bib19); [Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib51)). Learned evaluators offer broader coverage but may
introduce biases or incorrect judgments ([Zheng et al.,
2023](#bib.bib41)).

UnifiedPlayers treats executable evaluation as an adaptive role rather
than a fixed reward mechanism. The Evaluation Player generates verifiers
that are executed on original and perturbed trajectories. Their verdicts
form shared evidence from which separate Planning, Execution, and
Evaluation rewards are derived. The players retain separate parameters
and objectives and are updated in alternating blocks. Thus, cooperation
refers to the use of common executable evidence, not to a shared scalar
reward or shared policy parameters. This design complements
execution-centered tool-integrated reinforcement learning and two-player
self-evolving systems by explicitly modeling the interaction among
adaptive task generation, execution, and evaluation.

## Appendix B Methodology Details

### B.1 Cross-Player Interaction Records and Executable Feedback

Each task produces a cross-player interaction record that connects the
three policies through executable evidence. The Planning Player supplies
task $`q`$, the Execution Player samples $`K`$ original trajectories,
and the Evaluation Player generates $`M`$ candidate Python verifiers. A
fixed perturbation engine then produces $`P`$ variants of each
trajectory. After parsing and compilation, the sandbox executes every
valid verifier on the original and perturbed trajectories. We call the
resulting pass/fail outcomes executable feedback because they are
obtained by running verifier code rather than from unexecuted critiques
or another player’s reward.

Let $`\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{valid}}(q)`$ denote the valid verifier
indices and $`M_{q}=|\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{valid}}(q)|`$. For a completed
evaluation, $`v_{i}(\tau)`$ is the binary acceptance verdict. We record

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
Z^{\mathrm{orig}}_{i,k}=v_{i}(\tau_{k}),\qquad Z^{\mathrm{adv}}_{i,k,j}=v_{i}(\tau^{\mathrm{adv}}_{k,j}).
``` |  | (9) |

Flattening the adversarial trajectory indices $`(k,j)`$ gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbf{Z}(q)=[\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{orig}}\mid\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{adv}}]\in\{0,1\}^{M_{q}\times K(1+P)}.
``` |  | (10) |

Each row records one verifier’s judgments, while each column records the
verifier pool’s judgments of one trajectory. The columns therefore
provide feedback about Execution outputs, the rows provide feedback
about Evaluation outputs, and summaries across both inform Planning.

For $`M_{q}>0`$, the Execution reward averages the original-trajectory
column corresponding to its output. The Evaluation reward uses the row
summaries

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho_{i}^{\mathrm{gold}}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}Z^{\mathrm{orig}}_{i,k},\qquad\rho_{i}^{\mathrm{adv}}=\frac{1}{KP}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{j=1}^{P}(1-Z^{\mathrm{adv}}_{i,k,j}).
``` |  | (11) |

Here, $`\rho_{i}^{\mathrm{gold}}`$ measures acceptance of original
trajectories and $`\rho_{i}^{\mathrm{adv}}`$ measures rejection of their
perturbations. The superscript $`\mathrm{gold}`$ does not imply
independently verified correctness: an original trajectory may contain
an error, and a perturbation may preserve its correctness.

The Planning reward combines execution uncertainty, verifier
writability, and question repetition. Its verifier-writability term can
equivalently be written as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
V(q)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{valid}}(q)}\rho_{i}^{\mathrm{adv}}.
``` |  | (12) |

This form incorporates the valid-verifier fraction and gives $`V(q)=0`$
when no valid verifier is produced. Evaluation additionally uses
source-code redundancy, which is computed separately from the verdict
matrix.

The cross-player record $`\xi(q)`$ in
Eq. [1](#S3.E1 "In 3.1 Unified Cooperation under Executable Feedback ‣ 3 Method ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
collects $`q`$, the original trajectories $`\mathcal{T}(q)`$, valid
verifiers $`\mathcal{V}(q)`$, perturbed trajectories
$`\mathcal{T}^{\mathrm{adv}}(q)`$, verdict matrix $`\mathbf{Z}(q)`$, and
redundancy scores $`\bm{\rho}^{\mathrm{red}}(q)`$. Planning, Execution,
and Evaluation derive different rewards from this shared record. It
therefore coordinates the players through common executable evidence
without introducing a shared scalar reward, a new sequential rollout, or
gradient propagation across policies.

### B.2 The Objectives of UnifiedPlayers

Let $`\mathcal{X}`$ denote the interaction process induced by the three
policies, the perturbation engine, and the sandbox. The conditional
expected utilities are

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle J_{T}(\pi_{T};\pi_{S},\pi_{C})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{X}}[r_{T}(q)],`$ |  | (13) |
|  | $`\displaystyle J_{S}(\pi_{S};\pi_{T},\pi_{C})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{X}}[r_{S}(\tau)],`$ |  | (14) |
|  | $`\displaystyle J_{C}(\pi_{C};\pi_{T},\pi_{S})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{X}}[r_{C}(v)].`$ |  | (15) |

Each expectation includes the sampled tasks, trajectories, verifier
pools, and perturbations needed to evaluate that role’s reward. The
Planning objective also depends on the question history used by its
repetition penalty.

These objectives are coupled through shared evidence. Planning changes
the task distribution, Execution changes the trajectories being checked,
and Evaluation changes the executable judgments. Cooperation therefore
does not imply identical rewards or improvement in every utility after
each update. We assume neither a common scalar potential nor a shared
policy parameterization.

The mean of block surrogates in
Eq. [7](#S3.E7 "In 3.3 Alternating Cooperative Optimization ‣ 3 Method ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
is a reporting convention, not a shared training loss. Its factor of
$`1/3`$ does not prescribe gradient scaling in the optimizer. Each block
optimizes the active player’s own surrogate.

### B.3 Complete Policy Optimization Definitions

For active player $`p\in\{T,S,C\}`$ in block $`b`$, a group contains
candidate outputs generated under the same input context

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{G}_{p}(x)=\{(a_{p,g},r_{p,g})\}_{g=1}^{G_{p}},\qquad(x,\mathcal{G}_{p}(x))\in\mathcal{D}_{p}^{(b)}.
``` |  | (16) |

For Planning, $`x`$ is the fixed questioner prompt and $`a_{T,g}`$ is a
generated task with its expected answer. For Execution, $`x`$ is task
$`q`$ and $`a_{S,g}`$ is a sampled trajectory. For Evaluation, $`x`$
contains $`q`$ and the trajectory schema, and $`a_{C,g}`$ is a verifier
candidate. Other players’ outputs provide reward evidence but are not
members of the active player’s group.

Let $`\bar{r}_{p}`$ and $`s_{p}`$ denote the mean and standard deviation
of the rewards in this group. The candidate advantage is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widehat{A}_{p,g}=\frac{r_{p,g}-\bar{r}_{p}}{s_{p}+\epsilon},\qquad\epsilon>0.
``` |  | (17) |

The constant $`\epsilon`$ stabilizes the denominator. Under this
expression, equal rewards yield zero advantages. This removes the
reward-dependent term for that group, but the KL penalty can still
contribute to optimization.

The current policy $`\pi_{\theta_{p}}`$ is optimized against outputs
sampled by the behavior policy $`\pi_{p}^{\mathrm{old}}`$. The separate
reference policy $`\pi_{p}^{\mathrm{ref}}`$ is saved at the start of the
outer iteration and defines the KL penalty. Behavior-policy
probabilities remain fixed when optimizing the records they generated.
They are not interchangeable with reference-policy probabilities.

Let $`a_{p,g,t}`$ be a token at a position included in the candidate
loss, and let $`h_{p,g,t}`$ be its observed history. For Execution, this
history includes returned tool observations. The likelihood ratio is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\varrho_{p,g,t}(\theta_{p})=\frac{\pi_{\theta_{p}}(a_{p,g,t}\mid h_{p,g,t})}{\pi_{p}^{\mathrm{old}}(a_{p,g,t}\mid h_{p,g,t})}.
``` |  | (18) |

Its clipped value is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{\varrho}_{p,g,t}=\operatorname{clip}(\varrho_{p,g,t},1-\epsilon_{\mathrm{clip}},1+\epsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}).
``` |  | (19) |

Writing $`D^{\mathrm{KL}}_{p,g,t}`$ for the KL penalty relative to
$`\pi_{p}^{\mathrm{ref}}`$ at the same history, the token surrogate is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\ell_{p,g,t}=\min\!\left(\varrho_{p,g,t}\widehat{A}_{p,g},\bar{\varrho}_{p,g,t}\widehat{A}_{p,g}\right)-\beta_{p}D^{\mathrm{KL}}_{p,g,t}.
``` |  | (20) |

The candidate advantage is shared across its token positions. If
$`L_{p,g}`$ is the number of positions included in its loss, the full
block objective is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{J}_{p}^{(b)}(\theta_{p})=\mathbb{E}_{(x,\mathcal{G}_{p}(x))\sim\mathcal{D}_{p}^{(b)}}\left[\frac{1}{G_{p}}\sum_{g=1}^{G_{p}}\frac{1}{L_{p,g}}\sum_{t=1}^{L_{p,g}}\ell_{p,g,t}\right].
``` |  | (21) |

Thus, tokens are averaged within each candidate, candidates are averaged
within each group, and groups are averaged over the block data. Rewards
and advantages are not normalized across different roles.

### B.4 Update Order within UnifiedPlayers

An outer iteration contains three role blocks in the order Planning,
Execution, and Evaluation. A block contains multiple optimizer steps,
not a single update.
Table [6](#A4.T6 "Table 6 ‣ D.1 Hyperparameter Settings ‣ Appendix D Experimental Setup Details ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
specifies 200 Planning updates, 300 Execution updates, and 200
Evaluation updates per outer iteration. Training uses three outer
iterations.

#### Planning block.

The Execution and Evaluation policies remain fixed. Candidate tasks are
assessed using their trajectories, verifier judgments, and the question
repetition penalty. Only the Planning policy receives parameter updates.

#### Execution block.

The updated Planning policy supplies fresh tasks. Planning and
Evaluation remain fixed while Execution generates trajectories and is
optimized using acceptance judgments from the verifier pool.

#### Evaluation block.

Planning and the updated Execution policy remain fixed. Evaluation
generates verifier candidates, which are scored on original and
perturbed trajectories. Only Evaluation receives parameter updates. Its
resulting checkpoint is available to the other players in the next outer
iteration.

In Full UnifiedPlayers, each later block uses checkpoints updated
earlier in the same outer iteration: Execution receives tasks from
updated Planning, and Evaluation receives trajectories from updated
Execution. The stale-feedback control instead generates all tasks,
trajectories, verifiers, and verdict records using snapshots taken at
the start of the iteration. Therefore, its within-iteration updates do
not change another player’s interaction evidence until the next
iteration. This distinction concerns checkpoints used to generate
cross-player interaction records, not the reference checkpoints saved
for KL regularization.

Fixing the other players’ parameters does not require one dataset to
remain unchanged throughout all optimizer steps in a role block. The
fixed-record analysis below applies when optimizing sampled records and
does not assume that records are never refreshed.

## Appendix C Evaluation Metrics

### C.1 Player Coordination Protocol

#### Factorial configurations.

Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Implementation Details. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
compares four configurations on Qwen3-4B-Base. Execution is trained
throughout, while Planning and Evaluation independently remain frozen or
receive updates. A frozen player retains its initial checkpoint, prompt,
sampling budget, and forward generation process. It continues to provide
tasks or verifiers but receives no parameter updates. All configurations
use three outer iterations and matched task and sampling budgets. Saved
updates are not reassigned to Execution. Matching these budgets does not
require identical generated tasks, since adapting Planning changes the
task distribution.

#### Paired contrasts.

For each task family, let $`Y_{ab,s}`$ denote the benchmark average for
paired seed $`s`$, where $`a`$ and $`b`$ indicate whether Planning and
Evaluation are trainable. A value of zero denotes Frozen and one denotes
Trainable. We compute the marginal effects within each seed

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\Delta_{T,s}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{(Y_{10,s}-Y_{00,s})+(Y_{11,s}-Y_{01,s})}{2},`$ |  | (22) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\Delta_{C,s}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{(Y_{01,s}-Y_{00,s})+(Y_{11,s}-Y_{10,s})}{2}.`$ |  | (23) |

Each marginal averages a player’s effect over the other player’s two
settings. Their interaction is

|     |                                            |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       I_{s}=Y_{11,s}-Y_{10,s}-Y_{01,s}+Y_{00,s}.
       ```                                         |     | (24) |

This contrast measures departure from additivity on the reported score
scale. A positive sample interaction alone does not establish a general
benefit beyond the tested configurations and seeds.

For any configuration score or contrast $`z_{s}`$, we report the mean
and sample standard deviation over the three paired seeds

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{z}=\frac{1}{3}\sum_{s=1}^{3}z_{s},\qquad\operatorname{SD}(z)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\sum_{s=1}^{3}(z_{s}-\bar{z})^{2}}.
``` |  | (25) |

Contrasts are computed before aggregation. Their standard deviations
therefore come from paired differences, not from combining the
configuration-level standard deviations as if the runs were independent.

#### Fresh versus stale feedback.

The coordination comparison trains all three players with the same
initialization, prompts, reward definitions, update budgets, and task
and sampling budgets. Full UnifiedPlayers uses updated Planning outputs
in the Execution block and updated Execution outputs in the Evaluation
block.

The stale-feedback control snapshots all three policies at the start of
an outer iteration. These checkpoints generate the tasks, trajectories,
verifiers, and verdict records before the role updates. Each player then
performs its assigned updates using these records. Updated checkpoints
become available to the other players only in the next outer iteration.

Let $`Y_{\mathrm{stale},s}`$ denote the control’s score for seed $`s`$.
The paired coordination contrast is

|     |                                      |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       F_{s}=Y_{11,s}-Y_{\mathrm{stale},s}.
       ```                                   |     | (26) |

We summarize this contrast using
Eq. [25](#A3.E25 "In Paired contrasts. ‣ C.1 Player Coordination Protocol ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Metrics ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning"),
separately for mathematical and general reasoning.

#### Scope of the comparisons.

The factorial configurations preserve the executable-feedback pipeline
but do not use equal total compute. Their contrasts measure the effect
of adapting each role under the specified update allocation. Full and
stale-feedback UnifiedPlayers instead train the same roles with matching
update and sampling budgets and are both reported at 432 local GPU-hours
per seed. This comparison tests fresh alternating feedback against the
specified stale-feedback procedure, not against every possible
independent-training design.

### C.2 Coupled Learning Dynamics

Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")(a)
tracks three different process measures. Execution accuracy measures
task-solving performance. Evaluation adversarial rejection measures
rejection of perturbed trajectories, rather than discrimination across
both original and perturbed trajectories. For a task $`q`$, Planning
uncertainty is $`U(q)=\min(\hat{p},1-\hat{p})`$, where $`\hat{p}`$ is
the fraction of Execution samples sharing the most frequent answer.
Higher uncertainty indicates lower answer agreement, not independently
established task difficulty.

These measures should not be combined into a single team score. The
Execution curve is also distinct from the seven-benchmark Math AVG in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Block-wise optimization stability. ‣ 3.3 Alternating Cooperative Optimization ‣ 3 Method ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning").
Their simultaneous increases describe the observed training process but
do not identify individual causal contributions. We use the factorial
contrasts and fresh-versus-stale comparison in
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Player Coordination Protocol ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Metrics ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
to address attribution and coordination.

## Appendix D Experimental Setup Details

### D.1 Hyperparameter Settings

Table [6](#A4.T6 "Table 6 ‣ D.1 Hyperparameter Settings ‣ Appendix D Experimental Setup Details ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
lists the per-policy training hyperparameters used by UnifiedPlayers.
All three policies share a common AdamW optimizer ([Loshchilov and
Hutter, 2019](#bib.bib43)) with $`\beta_{1}=0.9`$, $`\beta_{2}=0.95`$,
weight decay 0.01, and gradient clipping at L2 norm 1.0. The Execution
Player receives more updates per outer iteration than the other two
because each of its rollouts is a multi-turn trajectory with tool calls,
which provides denser learning signal than the single-shot outputs of
the Planning or Evaluation Player. The Planning Player reward weights
are $`w_{\text{unc}}=1.0`$, $`w_{\text{ver}}=1.0`$,
$`w_{\text{rep}}=0.5`$ for the uncertainty, verifier-writability, and
BLEU-based repetition terms, and the Evaluation Player reward weights
are $`\alpha=0.4`$, $`\beta=0.5`$, $`\gamma=0.1`$ for the gold-pass,
adversarial-rejection, and redundancy terms
(Section[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Cooperative Players with Role-Specific Objectives ‣ 3 Method ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")).
We run three outer iterations in total. At the start of each outer
iteration the policy parameters become the new reference for the KL
term, and the Planning Player draws a fresh pool of approximately 1,000
questions per iteration.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| Hyperparameter | Planning | Execution | Evaluation |
| Learning rate | $`5\times 10^{-7}`$ | $`1\times 10^{-6}`$ | $`5\times 10^{-7}`$ |
| GRPO group size $`G`$ | 8 | 8 | 4 |
| Sampling temperature | 1.0 | 1.0 | 0.7 |
| Top-$`p`$ | 1.0 | 1.0 | 0.95 |
| Max response tokens | 512 | 4096 | 1024 |
| KL coefficient | 0.001 | 0.001 | 0.001 |
| PPO clipping radius | 0.2 | 0.2 | 0.2 |
| Updates per outer iteration | 200 | 300 | 200 |

Table 6: Per-policy training hyperparameters in UnifiedPlayers.

### D.2 Optimization Stability Diagnostics

We collect optimization diagnostics for the four player-attribution
configurations on Qwen3-4B-Base. Each policy update records the global
gradient norm before clipping, realized token-level KL relative to the
reference checkpoint at the start of the current outer iteration, the
fraction of sampled token ratios outside the PPO clipping interval, and
token entropy. Entropy is evaluated on fixed role-specific prompts and
reported as the final-to-initial ratio. Statistics are first computed
separately for each role, outer iteration, and paired seed before
aggregation. Raw values are compared only within the same role because
the players use different group sizes and output lengths. For gradient
statistics, the nine seed-by-iteration blocks receive equal weight. The
reported median and coefficient of variation aggregate the corresponding
block-level summaries. For realized KL and clipping fraction, each seed
first averages its three iteration-level summaries, after which we
report the mean across paired seeds. For entropy retention, each role
uses a fixed bank of 256 held-out contexts. Each seed first computes the
ratio between final and initial mean token entropy, and we then report
the mean across paired seeds.

Execution performance is evaluated every 50 updates on a fixed
diagnostic pool containing 128 held-out mathematical questions and 128
held-out general-reasoning questions. The initial checkpoint at update
zero is also evaluated, giving 19 checkpoints and 18 adjacent
comparisons over 900 Execution updates for each seed. This pool is used
only to measure training dynamics and is not used for checkpoint
selection, early stopping, or hyperparameter tuning. Negative-step rate
is the fraction of adjacent diagnostic checkpoints whose accuracy
decreases. Maximum drop is the largest such decrease in accuracy points.

| Role | Configuration | Grad. Median | CV | KL | Clip Fraction | Entropy Ret. |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Execution | Execution only | 0.86 | 0.37 | 0.018 | 0.16 | 0.91 |
| Execution | Planning + Execution | 0.79 | 0.35 | 0.016 | 0.13 | 0.91 |
| Execution | Execution + Evaluation | 0.77 | 0.32 | 0.016 | 0.15 | 0.90 |
| Execution | Full UnifiedPlayers | 0.73 | 0.31 | 0.014 | 0.09 | 0.87 |

Table 7: Execution Player optimization diagnostics across four training
configurations. Gradient statistics report the median pre-clipping
global norm and its coefficient of variation. Entropy retention is the
final-to-initial token-entropy ratio.

| Configuration          | Negative-Step Rate | Maximum Drop |
|------------------------|--------------------|--------------|
| Execution only         | 0.24               | 1.1          |
| Planning + Execution   | 0.20               | 0.9          |
| Execution + Evaluation | 0.17               | 0.8          |
| Full UnifiedPlayers    | 0.19               | 0.6          |

Table 8: Execution Player performance dynamics. Negative-step rate is
the fraction of adjacent diagnostic checkpoints with decreasing

For the Execution Player,
Tables [7](#A4.T7 "Table 7 ‣ D.2 Optimization Stability Diagnostics ‣ Appendix D Experimental Setup Details ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
and [8](#A4.T8 "Table 8 ‣ D.2 Optimization Stability Diagnostics ‣ Appendix D Experimental Setup Details ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
show lower gradient variability, realized KL, clipping frequency, and
maximum checkpoint decline in Full UnifiedPlayers than in the other
configurations. Entropy retention is lower, however, and the
negative-step rate slightly exceeds that of Execution + Evaluation.
These observations support reduced variability on several measures, but
do not establish uniformly better stability, monotonic team improvement,
or convergence.

### D.3 Sandbox Configuration

The sandbox is provided by VeRL-Tool ([Jiang et al., 2025](#bib.bib42))
and isolates each Python call in its own subprocess. Every call inherits
a fresh environment with no filesystem access outside the working
directory and no network access. We set a per-call wall-clock timeout of
10 seconds and a memory cap of 512 MB. Any call that exceeds either
limit is killed and recorded as a failure, with the exit status
propagated back to the calling policy. Allowed libraries are restricted
to the Python standard library, which prevents the Evaluation Player
from depending on heavy scientific packages whose presence might differ
across evaluation environments. The Execution Player emits code as
fenced Python blocks, and VeRL-Tool parses these blocks, executes them,
and returns the standard output, standard error, and exit status to the
Execution Player as the next observation. Verifier execution follows the
same protocol but runs in parallel processes so that all $`M`$ verifiers
can be applied to the original trajectory and its five perturbed
variants without serial overhead. For each task, the sandbox runs
$`K\cdot M\cdot(1+P)=192`$ executions in total, corresponding to $`K=8`$
Execution Player trajectories each evaluated by $`M=4`$ verifiers on the
original and on each of $`P=5`$ perturbed variants.

## Appendix E Prompt Templates

We lists the prompt templates used by the three policies. Placeholders
shown as {...} are filled in at training time. The Planning and
Evaluation Player prompts remain unchanged across all three outer
iterations, while the Execution Player prompt varies only in the
embedded problem statement.

### E.1 Planning Player Prompt

The Planning Player is prompted to generate a math problem together with
its expected answer, following the question-and-answer format used by
Agent0 ([Xia et al., 2025](#bib.bib20)). The prompt encourages problems
with verifiable single-value answers, namely integers, simple fractions,
or short closed-form expressions, and asks for multi-step reasoning
across a rotating set of topic categories. The expected answer is used
during data filtering to discard generations whose own claimed answer is
malformed, but it is not visible to the Execution or Evaluation Player
during training.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### E.2 Execution Player Prompt

The Execution Player is prompted to solve a task using natural-language
reasoning interleaved with Python tool calls. The prompt instructs the
model to enclose any code inside fenced Python blocks whose standard
output will be returned as the next observation, and to commit to a
final answer only when ready. Each Python call is dispatched to the
VeRL-Tool sandbox described in
Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Sandbox Configuration ‣ Appendix D Experimental Setup Details ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning").

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### E.3 Evaluation Player Prompt

The Evaluation Player is prompted to write a self-contained Python
verifier for the task. The prompt provides a schema describing the
trajectory data structure but does not reveal the Planning Player’s
expected answer, so the verifier must derive correctness from the
problem statement itself rather than memorizing a target value. The
Evaluation Player produces $`M=4`$ candidate verifiers per task, each
parsed and compiled independently before sandbox execution.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Appendix F Perturbation Engine Details

The perturbation engine creates adversarial variants of each Execution
Player trajectory by applying a fixed set of mutation rules at the step
level. Its purpose is to provide the Evaluation Player with a stable
stream of hard negatives, since an Evaluation Player that only sees
correct trajectories has no incentive to write verifiers that reject
anything. We use five rules in total, classified into Local edits that
modify a single step and Global edits that change the trajectory
structure. The rules are applied independently to every Execution Player
trajectory, so each trajectory generates exactly five perturbed variants
per outer iteration.

| Rule | Category |  Action |
|----|----|----|
| arg_mutation | Local |  Replace one numerical argument in a code step by a small perturbation. |
| step_drop | Local |  Remove one reasoning step from the trajectory. |
| step_swap | Local |  Swap the order of two adjacent steps. |
| early_terminate | Global |  Truncate the trajectory and inject a wrong final answer. |
| tool_substitute | Global |  Replace the declared tool type in a code step while keeping the code body unchanged. |

Table 9: The five mutation rules used by the perturbation engine.

### F.1 Five Mutation Rules

Table [9](#A6.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix F Perturbation Engine Details ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
summarizes the five rules. We describe the implementation of each below.

arg_mutation. The rule scans the trajectory for code steps containing
numerical literals, picks one literal uniformly at random, and replaces
it with a perturbed value (an additive offset in $`\{-2,-1,+1,+2\}`$ for
integers, or a $`\pm 5\%`$ shift for floats). The modified code is
re-executed in the sandbox, and its new output replaces the
corresponding recorded output.

step_drop. The rule selects one step of type reason uniformly at random
and removes it. Code and output steps are never dropped, since doing so
would leave an orphan output without a preceding code step.

step_swap. The rule selects a pair of adjacent steps and swaps their
positions. When a swap would split a code step from its output, the two
are first grouped as a single unit and that unit is swapped with the
neighboring step, preserving the input-output binding.

early_terminate. The rule picks a cut point at a random step before the
original final answer, discards every step after the cut, and appends a
fabricated final answer drawn from a small set of plausible distractors
such as off-by-one neighbors of the true answer or zero.

tool_substitute. The rule selects one code step at random and replaces
its language identifier, for example changing python to bash, while
leaving the code body and the original output unchanged. The perturbed
trajectory thus declares an invalid tool type relative to its observed
execution result.

### F.2 Before-After Examples

Table [10](#A6.T10 "Table 10 ‣ F.2 Before-After Examples ‣ Appendix F Perturbation Engine Details ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
shows one concrete before-after example for each of the five rules,
applied to the Execution Player trajectory on the MATH-500 problem from
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.5 Mechanism Analysis and Qualitative Case Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning").
Each row shows only the part of the trajectory that the rule changes.
All other steps are preserved verbatim.

## Appendix G Baselines and Benchmarks

### G.1 Baselines Overview

We compare UnifiedPlayers against six baselines that cover both the
no-training references and the strongest self-evolving frameworks in the
recent literature.

Vanilla. A reference point that runs the backbone without any
post-training and without tool use. The model is given the test problem
directly and must answer using only its pre-trained reasoning ability.

Tool-augmented. The same backbone as Vanilla, but with access to the
Python sandbox during inference. No post-training is applied, so any
gains over Vanilla reflect the value of code execution alone.

Absolute Zero ([Zhao et al., 2025](#bib.bib16)). The original method
uses one model to propose and solve code reasoning tasks without
externally supplied training questions. A code execution environment
validates generated tasks and provides reference outcomes for computing
rewards.

R-Zero ([Huang et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)). The original method
initializes separate Challenger and Solver policies from the same base
model and alternates their training. The Challenger proposes tasks near
the Solver’s capability boundary, while the Solver learns from
pseudo-labels obtained by majority voting over its sampled answers.

Socratic-Zero ([Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib17)). The original method
uses a Teacher with fixed parameters to evaluate solutions and refine
problems. The Solver learns from this feedback, while the Generator
learns to reproduce the Teacher’s problem-generation strategy. The
reported experiments use MATH seed questions and supervised
initialization of the Solver.

Agent0 ([Xia et al., 2025](#bib.bib20)). The closest precursor to
UnifiedPlayers, Agent0 alternates GRPO training of Curriculum and
Executor policies. The Curriculum reward combines Executor
self-consistency and tool-call frequency, while the Executor learns from
majority-vote pseudo-labels derived from its own sampled answers.

Baseline numbers on both backbones in
Tables [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Block-wise optimization stability. ‣ 3.3 Alternating Cooperative Optimization ‣ 3 Method ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
and [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Implementation Details. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
are produced by our re-implementation under a unified evaluation
protocol with the same prompts, decoding settings, and tool sandbox
across all methods.

### G.2 Evaluation Benchmarks

We evaluate on seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks and five
general-domain reasoning benchmarks.
Table [11](#A7.T11 "Table 11 ‣ G.2 Evaluation Benchmarks ‣ Appendix G Baselines and Benchmarks ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
summarizes the size and evaluation protocol of each, followed by short
descriptions.

| Benchmark      | Domain  | Test size | Difficulty level           | Metric  |
|----------------|---------|-----------|----------------------------|---------|
| AMC            | Math    | 40        | High-school competition    | mean@32 |
| MATH-500       | Math    | 500       | Mixed Levels 1–5           | pass@1  |
| GSM8K          | Math    | 1,319     | Grade school               | pass@1  |
| Minerva        | Math    | 272       | Undergraduate STEM         | pass@1  |
| Olympiad-Bench | Math    | 675       | Olympiad                   | pass@1  |
| AIME24         | Math    | 30        | Top-tier competition       | mean@32 |
| AIME25         | Math    | 30        | Top-tier competition       | mean@32 |
| SuperGPQA      | General | 26,529    | Graduate multi-domain      | pass@1  |
| MMLU-Pro       | General | 12,032    | Multi-discipline           | pass@1  |
| BBEH           | General | 4,520     | Hard reasoning             | pass@1  |
| GPQA-D         | General | 198       | Graduate science           | pass@1  |
| HumanEval      | Code    | 164       | Function-level programming | pass@1  |

Table 11: Statistics of the twelve evaluation benchmarks.

AMC ([Math AI, 2023](#bib.bib56)). The 40 problems from the 2023
American Mathematics Competition (AMC 10 and AMC 12 combined). These are
short-answer high-school competition problems. Due to the small problem
count we report mean@32.

MATH ([Hendrycks et al., 2021](#bib.bib32)). We use the MATH-500 subset,
a 500-problem cross-section of the original MATH dataset that spans
Levels 1 to 5 across the seven subjects of algebra, counting and
probability, geometry, intermediate algebra, number theory, prealgebra,
and precalculus.

GSM8K ([Cobbe et al., 2021](#bib.bib26)). A widely-used benchmark of
1,319 grade-school math word problems. Answers are integers and we
report pass@1 with greedy decoding.

Minerva ([Lewkowycz et al., 2022](#bib.bib33)). A 272-problem benchmark
covering undergraduate STEM topics, particularly calculus, linear
algebra, and physics word problems.

Olympiad-Bench ([He et al., 2024](#bib.bib34)). We use the English math
subset, which contains 675 problems drawn from mathematics olympiads
worldwide. Answers are short closed-form expressions or integers.

AIME24 ([Hugging Face H4, 2024](#bib.bib57)) and AIME25 ([Math AI,
2025](#bib.bib58)). The 30 problems from each year’s American
Invitational Mathematics Examination, the contest that selects top
high-school students for the USAMO. Answers are integers between 0 and
999. We report mean@32 due to the small problem count.

SuperGPQA ([M-A-P Team et al., 2025](#bib.bib35)). A 26,529-question
graduate-level benchmark spanning 285 disciplines. Each question is
multiple-choice with a structured option pool, designed to test
specialized knowledge that goes beyond standard undergraduate curricula.

MMLU-Pro ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib36)). A 12,032-question
multiple-choice benchmark spanning 14 disciplines including law,
economics, philosophy, and engineering. Each question has 10 options,
which makes random-guessing baselines weaker than on standard 4-option
MMLU.

BBEH ([Kazemi et al., 2025](#bib.bib37)). The BIG-Bench Extra Hard
benchmark, in which 23 of the hardest BIG-Bench reasoning tasks are
replaced by harder counterparts with stricter answer validation. The
benchmark totals 4,520 questions (22 tasks of 200 questions plus one
task of 120).

GPQA-D ([Rein et al., 2024](#bib.bib44)). A 198-question subset of GPQA
covering graduate-level biology, physics, and chemistry. Questions are
selected for high quality using expert agreement and difficulty for
non-experts with internet access. We report pass@1 with greedy decoding.

HumanEval ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib45)). A 164-problem programming
benchmark in which each task gives a Python function signature and
docstring and asks the model to produce a correct implementation.
Correctness is judged by running the produced code against the held-out
unit tests, and we report pass@1.
````
