### H.2 Compute Cost Comparison

Table [14](#A8.T14 "Table 14 ‣ H.2 Compute Cost Comparison ‣ Appendix H Additional Results and Analysis ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
reports local GPU-hours and final mathematical reasoning performance on
Qwen3-4B-Base. The runs use eight NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs, except
Socratic-Zero, which uses four local GPUs and an external grading API.
GPU-hours measure local GPU resource use rather than elapsed wall-clock
time or complete system cost. They do not separately quantify CPU
sandbox work or external API charges.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Method | Trained policies | Local GPU-hours | Math AVG | Gain vs Tool-aug. |
| Tool-augmented | – | – | 44.0 | – |
| \- Absolute Zero | 1 | 256 | 46.4 | +2.4 |
| \- R-Zero | 1 | 288 | 48.7 | +4.7 |
| \- Socratic-Zero | 1 (+ GPT-4o API) | 216 | 50.9 | +6.9 |
| \- Agent0 | 2 | 320 | 52.7 | +8.7 |
| \- UnifiedPlayers (ours) | 3 | 432 | 56.4 | +12.4 |

Table 14: Local compute cost and final math performance on
Qwen3-4B-Base. Math AVG is the average over the seven mathematical
benchmarks from
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Block-wise optimization stability. ‣ 3.3 Alternating Cooperative Optimization ‣ 3 Method ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning"),
and Gain vs Tool-augmented is measured against the Tool-augmented
reference (44.0).

For the attribution configurations in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Implementation Details. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning"),
Execution only, Planning + Execution, Execution + Evaluation, and Full
UnifiedPlayers are reported at 312, 360, 384, and 432 local GPU-hours
per seed, respectively. The stale-feedback control is also reported at
432 GPU-hours per seed. Thus, the factorial study matches task and
sampling budgets rather than total GPU cost, while the coordination
comparison additionally matches the reported GPU-hours.

Relative to Agent0, UnifiedPlayers uses 35% more reported local
GPU-hours. Dividing the mathematical reasoning gain over the
Tool-augmented reference by these costs gives approximately 0.029 points
per GPU-hour for UnifiedPlayers and 0.027 for Agent0. These ratios
describe the reported runs and should not be interpreted as a comparison
of total system cost.

### H.3 Perturbation Rule Subsets

This analysis extends the “w/o Perturbation Engine” comparison in
Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Individual Player contributions. ‣ 4.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
by separating the rules used in the full configuration into two subsets.

We divide the five perturbation rules into local and global subsets to
examine whether their effects are redundant. Local edits modify
individual reasoning or execution steps and include arg_mutation,
step_drop, and step_swap. Global edits change the trajectory structure
and include early_terminate and tool_substitute.

| Perturbation Rules          | Math AVG | Adv. Reject |
|-----------------------------|----------|-------------|
| Full capacity (5 rules)     | 56.4     | 0.79        |
| Local edits only (3 rules)  | 55.2     | 0.68        |
| Global edits only (2 rules) | 54.9     | 0.71        |
| No perturbation             | 51.6     | 0.21        |

Table 15: Effect of perturbation-rule subsets on Qwen3-4B-Base. Math AVG
measures downstream task performance, and Adv. Reject measures the
adversarial rejection rate of the Evaluation Player.

Table [15](#A8.T15 "Table 15 ‣ H.3 Perturbation Rule Subsets ‣ Appendix H Additional Results and Analysis ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
shows that the local subset retains a higher math average than the
global subset, whereas the global subset retains a higher adversarial
rejection rate. The full five-rule configuration performs best on both
measures. Removing all perturbations lowers Math AVG from 56.4 to 51.6
and adversarial rejection from 0.79 to 0.21. These results suggest that
local and global rules provide complementary negative examples, although
the subset comparison does not isolate the contribution of each
individual rule.

### H.4 Verifier Pool Size (M) Sweep

This sweep extends the “Single Verifier” comparison in
Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Individual Player contributions. ‣ 4.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
by varying the verifier-pool size over $`M\in\{1,2,4,8\}`$.
UnifiedPlayers uses $`M=4`$ Evaluation Player candidates per task in the
main experiments.
Table [16](#A8.T16 "Table 16 ‣ H.4 Verifier Pool Size (M) Sweep ‣ Appendix H Additional Results and Analysis ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
reports downstream performance and local compute cost on Qwen3-4B-Base.

| $`M`$    | Math AVG | General AVG | Local GPU-hours |
|----------|----------|-------------|-----------------|
| 1        | 54.3     | 44.2        | 356             |
| 2        | 55.4     | 45.3        | 388             |
| 4 (used) | 56.4     | 46.1        | 432             |
| 8        | 57.0     | 46.4        | 519             |

Table 16: Effect of Evaluation Player pool size $`M`$ on Qwen3-4B-Base.
The bold $`M=4`$ row is the setting used by UnifiedPlayers in
Tables [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Block-wise optimization stability. ‣ 3.3 Alternating Cooperative Optimization ‣ 3 Method ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
and [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Implementation Details. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning").

Within the tested range, larger verifier pools improve both benchmark
averages while increasing reported local GPU-hours. Increasing $`M`$
from 4 to 8 raises Math AVG from 56.4 to 57.0 and General AVG from 46.1
to 46.4, while GPU-hours increase from 432 to 519. The main setting
$`M=4`$ therefore provides a lower-cost alternative with smaller
performance differences than those observed between $`M=1`$ and $`M=4`$.
This comparison characterizes the tested settings and does not establish
an optimal pool size.

### H.5 Reward Coefficient Sensitivity

This analysis extends the “w/o Diversity Penalty” comparison in
Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Individual Player contributions. ‣ 4.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
and tests a broader range of Evaluation Player reward weights. The
reward in
Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Cooperative Players with Role-Specific Objectives ‣ 3 Method ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
combines gold-pass, adversarial-rejection, and redundancy terms with
default coefficients $`(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)=(0.4,0.5,0.1)`$. We vary
these weights on Qwen3-4B-Base and report the resulting performance in
Table [17](#A8.T17 "Table 17 ‣ H.5 Reward Coefficient Sensitivity ‣ Appendix H Additional Results and Analysis ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning").

| Configuration       | $`\alpha`$ | $`\beta`$ | $`\gamma`$ | Math AVG | General AVG |
|---------------------|------------|-----------|------------|----------|-------------|
| Default (used)      | 0.4        | 0.5       | 0.1        | 56.4     | 46.1        |
| Heavier gold-pass   | 0.6        | 0.3       | 0.1        | 55.7     | 45.4        |
| Heavier adversarial | 0.2        | 0.7       | 0.1        | 56.1     | 45.9        |
| Strong diversity    | 0.4        | 0.5       | 0.3        | 55.3     | 45.5        |
| No diversity        | 0.4        | 0.5       | 0.0        | 54.2     | 44.6        |

Table 17: Sensitivity to the Evaluation Player reward coefficients
$`(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)`$ on Qwen3-4B-Base. The bold default row is the
setting used by UnifiedPlayers in
Tables [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Block-wise optimization stability. ‣ 3.3 Alternating Cooperative Optimization ‣ 3 Method ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
and [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Implementation Details. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning").

All four variants remain within 2.2 points of the default on math and
1.5 points on general reasoning. Removing the diversity term produces
the largest decrease in this sweep. Increasing its weight to
$`\gamma=0.3`$ also reduces performance relative to the default. Among
the two rebalanced settings, the heavier adversarial weight performs
slightly better than the heavier gold-pass weight on both task families.
These results show moderate sensitivity within the tested range. They do
not establish robustness to reward settings outside this sweep or
isolate the effect of one coefficient when the others change.

### I.3 Illustrative Verifier Checks

For Trajectories 1, 2, 4, and 5 in
Appendix [I.2](#A9.SS2 "I.2 Execution Player Trajectory Examples ‣ Appendix I Case Analysis ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning"),
we present three illustrative checks per task. These listings show
individual acceptance conditions, not complete verifier implementations
or verbatim training outputs. Each function is named check_condition and
returns a Boolean result with a diagnostic message. This display format
is distinct from the formal check(trajectory) interface, which returns
(passed, fail_step) as specified in
Appendix [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Evaluation Player Prompt ‣ Appendix E Prompt Templates ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning").
The listings do not implement failure-step localization.

#### Input parsing.

The trajectory schema stores final_answer as a string. The numerical
checks illustrated in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.5 Mechanism Analysis and Qualitative Case Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ UnifiedPlayers: Enhance Tool-Integrated Reasoning in Agentic Reinforcement Learning")
therefore require integer conversion before divisibility or minimality
tests:

``` ltx_verbatim
 ans = int(trajectory.final_answer)
````

These checks have different limitations. Verifier 1.2 checks agreement
between the recorded output and final answer, but accepts an incorrect
value when both are 8 rather than 9. Verifier 4.1 checks only
$`N^{2}=121`$ and therefore accepts $`N=-11`$, although the task
requires a positive integer. Most other listings check the final answer
without validating every reasoning step. Agreement and answer checks
alone therefore do not establish trajectory correctness. The examples
illustrate possible failure modes of individual checks, not a guarantee
that a verifier pool eliminates them.
